results.question: Do creatures phasing back in trigger enter the battlefield abilities?
results.text:
No. A creature that phases in does not trigger enters-the-battlefield abilities. Phasing is not a zone change, and zone-change triggers (including “When/Whenever [this permanent] enters the battlefield” abilities) don’t trigger when a permanent phases in.

Definition of phasing (key points): Phasing is a status (phased in/phased out) that modifies the untap step; when a permanent phases out its status changes to “phased out” and, except for effects that specifically mention phased-out permanents, it’s treated as though it doesn’t exist; when a permanent phases in its status changes to “phased in” and the game treats it as though it exists again [702.26a][702.26b][702.26c].

Reasoning: Enters-the-battlefield abilities are zone-change triggers that trigger when a permanent actually enters the battlefield [603.6a]. Phasing does not put a permanent into or out of a zone; the phasing event “doesn’t actually cause a permanent to change zones” and “zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out” [702.26d]. Therefore a permanent phasing in is not the same event as a permanent entering the battlefield and won’t cause enters-the-battlefield triggers to trigger. Note that there is a separate exception for abilities that trigger when a permanent phases out: those abilities look back in time to determine whether they triggered [603.10b], but that exception doesn’t make phasing in count as entering the battlefield.

If you’re asking about a specific one-shot effect that phases a permanent back in (for example, an “until” effect that creates a second one-shot when its condition occurs), that still causes a phasing event rather than a zone change, so the same answer applies [610.4].

results.question: how does trample work with deathtouch?
results.text:
Short answer: When an attacking creature has both trample and deathtouch, you need only assign 1 point of combat damage to each blocking creature for assignment purposes; any remaining damage may be assigned as excess to the defending player or planeswalker (subject to the usual trample-over-planeswalkers rules). After damage is dealt, a creature dealt any nonzero damage by a source with deathtouch is destroyed as a state-based action.

Why: • Deathtouch makes any nonzero amount of damage be considered lethal for assignment purposes ([702.2c]). • Trample modifies how attacking creatures assign combat damage: the attacker must assign lethal damage to each blocking creature, then may assign excess damage to the player or planeswalker being attacked ([702.19a], [702.19b]). • Rule 120.4a specifically notes that when a source has deathtouch, any amount of damage greater than 1 is excess damage; thus only 1 point need be assigned to a blocking creature to count as lethal when the source has deathtouch ([120.4a]). • When assigning combat damage you follow the normal assignment step (each attacking creature assigns combat damage equal to its power) ([510.1a]). • When checking how much damage is lethal to blockers you take into account damage already marked on them and damage from other creatures being assigned in the same combat damage step ([702.19b], [120.6]).

What happens after damage is dealt: Damage dealt without wither or infect is marked on creatures ([302.7]). If a creature with toughness greater than 0 has been dealt damage by a source with deathtouch since the last time state-based actions were checked, that creature is destroyed as a state-based action ([702.2b], [704.5h]).

Planeswalker note: If the attacking creature has trample over planeswalkers, the same 1-damage-as-lethal rule for blockers applies, but you must also assign damage at least equal to the planeswalker’s loyalty (taking into account other simultaneous assignments) before assigning further excess to that planeswalker’s controller ([702.19c], [120.4a]).

Assumption about timing: This answer assumes you mean assignment of combat damage during the combat damage assignment step; if damage has already been marked on a blocker before assignment, that marked damage reduces how much you need to assign now as described above ([702.19b], [120.6]).

results.question: is storm a triggered ability that can be countered?
results.text:
Yes. Storm is a triggered ability, and the storm triggered ability (which functions on the stack) is an ability on the stack rather than a spell; it can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells but can be countered by effects that specifically counter abilities. 

Definitions and reasoning
- Storm: “Storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack. ‘Storm’ means ‘When you cast this spell, copy it for each other spell that was cast before it this turn. If the spell has any targets, you may choose new targets for any of the copies.’” [702.40a]
- Triggered ability: A triggered ability has a trigger condition and an effect and is written like “When/Whenever/At …, [effect].” Such an ability, once it triggers, is put on the stack as an object that’s not a card. [603.1a] [603.3] [603.3d]
- Whether it can be countered: Activated and triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells, so they can’t be countered by effects that counter only spells; they can be countered only by effects that specifically counter abilities. Because storm is a triggered ability that functions on the stack, it follows this rule. [113.9] [702.40a]

Assumption: I assume the question asks about the storm trigger itself (the triggered ability that creates copies). If you instead meant the spell that has storm, that spell is a spell on the stack while it’s being cast and may be countered by effects that counter spells (that’s a different object from the storm triggered ability). [601.2a]

results.question: can i use cards with hybrid mana symbols in a commander deck that only has one of those colors?
results.text:
Short answer: Generally no — a card with a hybrid mana symbol that includes a color not in your commander’s color identity is illegal in that commander deck. The only time a hybrid-symbol card is legal in a single-color commander deck is when every colored component of the hybrid symbol is a color that is in the commander’s color identity (for example, a monocolored hybrid like {2/G} counts only as green, so it’s fine in a green-only commander deck).

Definitions and rules used:
- Color identity: A card’s color identity is the color or colors of any mana symbols in that card’s mana cost or rules text (and other specific sources). This is what determines whether the card may be in a commander deck with a particular commander (see rule 903.4). [Definition: “color identity” per 903.4]
- Hybrid mana symbol: A hybrid mana symbol is a mana symbol that represents a cost that can be paid in one of two ways. A hybrid mana symbol is considered to be all of its component colors, and a monocolored hybrid symbol (for example, {2/G}) is a hybrid whose colored component is that single color (see rule 107.4e). [Definition: “hybrid mana symbol” per 107.4e]

How the rules apply:
- Because color identity includes the colors of mana symbols in a card’s mana cost or rules text, any colored components of a hybrid symbol become part of that card’s color identity (see rule 903.4 and rule 202.2d).
- Because a hybrid mana symbol is all of its component colors, a hybrid symbol that shows two different colors (for example {G/W}) makes the card both of those colors for color-identity purposes; such a card cannot be included in a commander deck whose commander’s color identity lacks one of those colors (see rule 107.4e and rule 903.4).
- A monocolored hybrid symbol (for example {2/G} or {C/G}) has only one colored component, so it adds only that single color to the card’s color identity. Such a card is legal in a commander deck whose commander’s color identity includes that single color (see rule 107.4e and rule 903.4).

Example summaries (assuming the usual timing/definitions):
- A card with mana cost including {G/W} has both green and white in its color identity, so it’s illegal in a green-only commander deck. (107.4e; 903.4)
- A card with mana cost including {2/G} has green in its color identity (the generic half doesn’t add a color), so it is legal in a green-only commander deck. (107.4e; 903.4)

results.question: can I respond to the untap step?
results.text:
No — you cannot respond during the untap step. No player receives priority during the untap step, so players can’t cast spells or activate abilities during that step (spells can’t be cast and abilities can’t be activated or resolve) ([502.4]; see also [500.3]).

Definition: “Respond to the untap step” means taking any action that requires having priority (for example, casting spells, activating abilities, or taking other actions that use the stack). Priority determines who may take those actions ([117.1]).

What happens to triggered abilities that occur during the untap step: any ability that triggers during the untap step is held until the next time a player would receive priority (this is usually during the upkeep step), at which point those triggered abilities are put onto the stack ([502.4]; [503.1a]).

Why you can’t act then: the untap step is one of the steps in which no player receives priority, so its turn-based actions happen automatically and don’t use the stack ([500.3]; [703.1]).

Assumption: I’m answering for the normal untap step as described in the rules provided. The answer is the same regardless of number of players because these rules don’t distinguish between two-player and multiplayer for priority during the untap step.

results.question: are creatures still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step?
results.text:
Yes. Creatures that were declared as attackers are still considered attacking creatures during the end of combat step, until they are removed from combat or the combat phase ends. 

Definition: “Attacking Creature. A creature that has either been declared as part of a legal attack during the combat phase (once all costs to attack, if any, have been paid), or a creature that has been put onto the battlefield attacking. It remains an attacking creature until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends, whichever comes first.” [Attacking Creature]

Reasoning: The Attacking Creature definition states that an attacking creature remains attacking until it’s removed from combat or the combat phase ends. Creatures are removed from combat as a turn-based action when the end of combat step ends (all creatures, battles, and planeswalkers are removed from combat as soon as the end of combat step ends). That means during the end of combat step itself they are still in combat and thus still attacking, unless some other effect removed them from combat earlier (for example, any of the conditions listed that remove a permanent from combat). [Attacking Creature; 511.3; 511.2; 511.1; 506.4a]

If an effect specifically removes a creature from combat (or the creature otherwise meets a removal-from-combat condition) before the end of combat step ends, that creature stops being an attacking creature immediately when it’s removed. [506.4a]

results.question: Do you cast lands?
results.text:
No — you do not cast lands. You play lands as a special action (not as spells).

Explanation and definitions (rules cited):
- Play a land: “To play a land means to put it onto the battlefield from the zone it’s in (usually the hand).” A player may play a land only any time they have priority during a main phase of their turn when the stack is empty and they haven’t played a land this turn. [701.18a] [116.2a]
- Playing a land is a special action and doesn’t use the stack; the land isn’t a spell and players can’t respond to playing it with instants or activated abilities. [305.1] [116.1]
- Lands normally have no mana cost and are played without paying any costs. (That’s why they aren’t cast like spells.) [202.1b]
- An object that is both a land and another card type can only be played as a land and can’t be cast as a spell. [305.9] [300.2a]
- Putting a land onto the battlefield because of a spell or ability (“put” effects) isn’t the same as playing a land. [305.4]
- By contrast, casting a spell (for example, casting a creature card) uses the stack. Casting is different from the special action of playing a land. [302.1] [117.1]
- In practice, the active player gets priority during a main phase and may play a land if the other conditions are met. [505.6b]

Assumption: This answer uses the timing rules above (main phase, priority, empty stack) as the conditions for playing lands; if those conditions aren’t met, you can’t play a land. [701.18a]

results.question: can I sacrifice an evoked creature before that creature's evoke triggered ability resolves?
results.text:
Yes. You may sacrifice a creature cast for its Evoke cost after it has entered the battlefield but before the Evoke triggered ability resolves.

Definition: Evoke is a keyword that is both a static ability used to cast the card for an alternative cost and a triggered ability that functions on the battlefield; it reads in effect, “When this permanent enters, if its evoke cost was paid, its controller sacrifices it.” (See rule [702.74a].)

Explanation and assumptions: I’m assuming the normal timing where the creature has entered the battlefield, the Evoke triggered ability has triggered, and that triggered ability is waiting to be put on the stack or is already on the stack but hasn’t resolved yet. A triggered ability that triggers when the creature enters the battlefield is put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority (see rule [603.3d]), and objects on the stack resolve only after players pass priority (see rule [608.1]). While the Evoke triggered ability is on the stack (or waiting to be put on the stack), players can cast spells or activate abilities that cause sacrifices (sacrificing a permanent can be done as part of paying costs or as the result of spells/abilities paid/activated while you have priority; see rule [601.2h] for sacrifices as costs when casting).

If you cause the creature to be sacrificed before the Evoke triggered ability resolves, the Evoke triggered ability will still exist on the stack and will resolve later (abilities exist on the stack independently of their source; see rule [113.7a]). When that Evoke triggered ability resolves it will attempt to have its controller sacrifice the permanent, but if the creature is no longer on the battlefield the sacrifice option is not available (a player who can’t legally choose a sacrifice option can’t choose it; see rule [608.2d]).

In short: you can sacrifice the creature in response to its Evoke trigger; the trigger will still resolve afterward but can’t make you sacrifice that permanent again if it’s already gone.

results.question: if a card loses all abilities, does that include keyword abilities?
results.text:
Yes. "Loses all abilities" removes keyword abilities. A keyword is a named ability printed as a short name on a card (a "keyword") rather than full rules text [702.1]. An effect that removes abilities removes abilities of the object, and if it says an object "loses" an ability it removes all instances of that ability [113.10][113.10b]. Keyword abilities are abilities, so they are affected. Such ability-removing (and ability-adding) continuous effects are applied in layer 6 of the continuous-effects layering system [613.1f].

Two important qualifications: (1) Some things that look like abilities are not abilities for these purposes. An effect that simply states a quality of an object (for example, "[creature] can’t be blocked") is neither granting an ability nor setting a characteristic, so a "loses all abilities" effect wouldn’t remove that kind of quality [113.12]. (2) "This creature can’t block" is itself an ability, so it would be removed by an effect that makes the creature lose abilities [113.2a].

If an effect says an object "can’t have" a particular ability, that effect causes the object to lose that ability (and prevents it from gaining it) and is applied as part of ability-removing/ability-preventing effects in layer 6 [113.11][613.1f].

results.question: can i draw cards if i'm already at my maximum hand size?

Definition: a player’s maximum hand size is how many cards they’re allowed to keep at the end of turn (normally seven) and is enforced during the cleanup step (see rule 402.2). Note two related points: (1) if an instruction tells you to draw more cards than remain in your library, drawing the remaining cards may cause you to lose the game the next time a player would receive priority (see rule 104.3c), and (2) when instructed to draw multiple cards, do each draw one at a time (see rule 121.2b).

results.question: can you explain layers?
results.text:
Layers are the game’s system for determining the order in which continuous effects are applied to an object’s characteristics. Start with the object’s printed (or effect-defined) values, then apply continuous effects in the layer sequence; each layer and sublayer is applied in order to produce the object’s final characteristics. (This is the direct answer.)

What a “layer” is and how it’s used
- A layer is a step in a fixed sequence the game uses to apply continuous effects so they interact predictably. The process begins with the object’s actual printed or effect-defined values and then applies continuous effects in the layers listed by rule 613 (this ordering is what “layers” are). [613.1]
- The specific layers named in the rules include at least: Layer 1 (effects that modify copiable values), Layer 3 (text-changing effects), Layer 4 (type-changing effects), Layer 5 (color-changing effects), Layer 6 (ability-adding or -removing effects), and Layer 7 (power/toughness effects). Each of those layers is applied in that order. [613.1a] [613.1c] [613.1d] [613.1e] [613.1f]

How the application within and between layers works
- Within a layer (or sublayer), effects are normally applied in timestamp order: earlier timestamps are applied before later ones. [613.7]
- Some layers are subdivided (for example, Layer 1 and Layer 7 have sublayer structure). Within such sublayers you also use timestamp order unless dependency changes the order. [613.2a] [613.2c] [613.4a]
- Dependency can override timestamp order when one effect depends on another (dependency is tested within the same layer/sub‑layer). If dependency exists, the dependent effect is ordered so that the other effect is applied first. [613.8] [613.8a]
- In layers 2–6, characteristic-defining abilities are applied first in that layer, then other effects in timestamp order (subject to dependency). Characteristic-defining abilities can add or override characteristics and function in all zones. [613.3] [604.3]

Special notes and examples from the rules
- “Copiable values” are the values derived from the text printed on an object (name, mana cost, color indicator, card type, subtype, supertype, rules text, power, toughness, and/or loyalty) as modified by copy effects and certain “as … enters” or “as … is turned face up” effects. Layer 1 handles effects that modify those copiable values; after Layer 1 is applied, an object’s copiable values are set. [613.2a] [707.2]
- The application of continuous effects is continual and instantaneous: the game always performs this layer-based application to produce current characteristics. Examples in the rules show how changing a creature’s color (Layer 5) can cause an effect like Honor of the Pure’s “White creatures you control get +1/+1” to start or stop applying depending on the color result. [613.5] (See the cited example using Honor of the Pure and other provided examples.)
- If a single effect has parts that belong in different layers, each part is applied in its appropriate layer; the effect will continue to apply to the same set of objects across all applicable layers even if the ability that generated the effect is removed during the process. The rules’ examples include an effect that both changes control (Layer 2) and grants haste (Layer 6) such as Act of Treason. [613.6]

Putting it together (practical steps for resolving interactions)
1. Begin with the object’s printed or effect-defined characteristics. [613.1]
2. Apply Layer 1 effects (copiable-value modifications and sublayers) to determine copiable values. [613.2a] [613.2c]
3. Apply Layers 2–6 in order, remembering that in those layers characteristic-defining abilities apply first in that layer, then other effects by timestamp (dependency may change order). [613.3] [613.7] [613.8]
4. Apply Layer 7’s sublayers in their order (characteristic-defining P/T first in 7a, then other P/T changes, counters, and so on), again using timestamp and dependency rules inside sublayers. [613.4a] [613.7] [613.8]
5. The result after all layers is the object’s current characteristics; the game continuously and instantaneously recalculates this as effects begin, end, or change. [613.5]

If you want concrete walkthroughs, the rules give several examples you can follow (for example, Honor of the Pure; Gray Ogre; Act of Treason; Svogthos, the Restless Tomb; Chimeric Staff; Clone) showing how particular changes are applied across layers. [613.5] [613.6] [707.2]

Assumption about timing: I described the canonical layer-application sequence as the rules do (the game continuously applies layers); if you meant “what happens at a single instant after a spell resolves” the same layer rules determine the final characteristics immediately after that resolution. The outcome can differ only if the timing you meant involves a different set of effects being present when the recalculation occurs. [613.6]

Direct answer: When a player controls two or more legendary permanents that share the same name, the legend rule (a state-based action) makes that player choose one of those permanents and put all the others into their owners’ graveyards [Legend Rule] [704.5j].

Definitions and how it works in play:
- “Legendary permanent” means any permanent with the supertype “legendary” [205.4d].
- A state-based action is a game action that happens automatically whenever its conditions are met and it doesn’t use the stack [704.1]. The legend rule is one of those state-based actions [704.5j].
- The choice of which legendary permanent to keep is made by the player who controls the multiple legendary permanents; the others are put into their owners’ graveyards as that state-based action resolves [704.5j].
- State-based actions (including the legend rule) are performed whenever the game would give priority, before triggered abilities are placed on the stack; see rule 117.5 for the timing of state-based-action checks and rule 117.2d for the fact that state-based actions are performed automatically [117.5] [117.2d].

results.question: when does my creature die after its been marked with a lethal amount of damage?
results.text:
Your creature is destroyed as a state-based action the next time the game checks state-based actions — i.e., as soon as state-based actions are checked after the damage is marked (which normally is immediately when a player would get priority). However, state-based actions aren’t checked in the middle of a spell or ability resolving, and during the cleanup step damage is removed before that cleanup check, so those timings can affect whether it dies then.

Reasoning and definitions
- State-based actions: game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met; they don’t use the stack and are performed whenever a player would get priority (definition and timing) [704.1][704.3][117.5][117.2d][405.6f].
- Lethal damage: damage is “lethal” for a creature when the total damage marked on that creature is greater than or equal to its toughness; such a creature is destroyed as a state-based action (regeneration can replace that event) [120.6][704.5g][302.7].
- Damage remains marked on a creature until it regenerates or until the cleanup step removes it; that marked damage is what state-based actions look at when determining lethal damage [120.6][514.2].

Practical summary of timings
- Normal case (most of the time): after damage is dealt and any spell or ability that dealt it finishes resolving, the game will check state-based actions before any player gets priority; if the total damage marked on the creature is ≥ its toughness, it is destroyed then [704.3][117.5][120.6][302.7].
- During resolution: state-based actions don’t pay attention to intermediate changes happening during a spell or ability’s resolution, so a creature won’t be destroyed mid-resolution because of temporary changes that haven’t “settled” when resolution finishes [704.4].
- Cleanup step: at the cleanup step all damage is removed as a turn-based action before the cleanup’s check for state-based actions and triggered abilities; so lethal damage that still exists at the start of cleanup will be removed by 514.2 before the cleanup’s SBA check, and the creature won’t be destroyed by that damage in that cleanup step [514.2][514.3a][703.4p].

results.question: can I cast my commander from exile?
results.text:
No — you can’t normally begin casting your commander while it is in exile. However, if your commander was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, you may put that commander into the command zone as a state-based action, and you may then cast that commander from the command zone (paying the commander’s additional {2} commander tax for each previous time you’ve cast it from the command zone this game).

Reasoning and definitions
- “State-based action” — game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met; they don’t use the stack [704.1].
- “Command zone” — a game area reserved for certain specialized objects that are not permanents [408.1].
- You can begin to cast a spell only if a rule or effect allows you to cast it and no rule or effect prohibits doing so [601.3e]; some rules specifically allow casting spells from exile, but you need such an allowance to cast from exile [601.3f]. If a card in exile is face down, players can’t look at it except as allowed by effects, and a player may only cast a face-down exiled card if they are allowed to look at it and the spell meets the required qualities [406.3b; 601.3f].
- Commander-specific interaction: If a commander is in exile and that object was put into exile since the last time state-based actions were checked, its owner may put that commander into the command zone as a state-based action [903.9a]. A commander may be cast from the command zone, with an additional {2} for each previous time it was cast from the command zone that game (the commander tax) [903.8].

Putting that together: there is no general rule that lets you cast a commander directly from exile. Instead, when the condition in [903.9a] applies (it was just put into exile), you may move that commander to the command zone via a state-based action and then cast it from the command zone under [903.8]. If some other effect specifically lets you cast that commander while it remains in exile, follow that effect and the casting rules in [601.3e] and [601.3f].

results.question: what happens during the cleanup step?
results.text:
Direct answer: During the cleanup step the active player first discards down to their maximum hand size, then all damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end. Normally no player gets priority during the cleanup step, but if state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting to be put onto the stack (including those that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), those state-based actions are performed, then those triggered abilities are put onto the stack, and then the active player gets priority; players may then cast spells and activate abilities. If the stack empties and all players pass in succession, another cleanup step begins. If, at the cleanup step’s first state-based-action check, no state-based actions are performed and no triggered abilities are waiting, then no player gets priority and the cleanup step ends. When the cleanup step ends, any unspent mana in players’ mana pools empties.

Definition and order of things (assumptions and sequence made explicit):
- The cleanup step is a step with turn-based actions that are dealt with immediately when it begins; those turn-based actions are handled before state-based actions are checked and before triggered abilities are put on the stack. The turn-based actions that happen during the cleanup step are:
  1) The active player discards down to their maximum hand size (this is a turn-based action that doesn’t use the stack). [514.1]
  2) All damage is removed from permanents and all “until end of turn” and “this turn” effects end; these happen simultaneously and don’t use the stack. [514.2] [703.4p]
- After those turn-based actions, the game checks for state-based actions and follows the cleanup-step priority exception process: if any state-based actions would be performed or any triggered abilities are waiting, perform those state-based actions, put waiting triggered abilities onto the stack, then the active player gets priority and players can act; repeat checks as required. If nothing needs to be done at the first check, no player gets priority and the step ends. [703.3] [514.3a] [514.3] [704.3]
- As the cleanup step (or any step/phase) ends, any unspent mana empties from players’ mana pools. [500.5] [703.4q]

Special note about effects that “end the turn”: if an effect ends the turn, follow the special end-the-turn process, which includes jumping to the cleanup step and a special handling of state-based actions and triggered abilities (no priority while the end-the-turn process is happening; triggered abilities that happened during that process are put onto the stack during the cleanup step, etc.). If an effect ends the turn during the cleanup step, a new cleanup step begins. [724.1c] [724.1d] [724.1f]
