results.question: when are state-based actions checked?
results.text:
State-based actions are checked any time a player would get priority; they’re also checked at step/phase boundaries after any turn-based actions are handled, and in certain special cases (for example, when an effect ends the turn or combat, or during the cleanup-step exception). See rules cited below for the exact ordering.

Definition: State-based actions are game actions that happen automatically whenever certain conditions are met; they don’t use the stack. (See rule [704.1].)

When and how they’re checked and applied
- The game checks for and performs all applicable state-based actions whenever a player would get priority, and repeats that check until no state-based actions are performed; after that, triggered abilities waiting to be put on the stack are put on the stack, and the process repeats until nothing more happens, at which point the appropriate player receives priority. (See rules [704.3] and [117.5].)
- State-based actions are checked throughout the game and are not controlled by any player. (See rule [704.2].)
- When a step or phase begins, any turn-based actions associated with that step or phase are dealt with first; that happens before state-based actions are checked. (See rule [703.3].) The active player normally receives priority at the beginning of steps and phases after those turn-based actions and after abilities that trigger at the beginning of the phase are put on the stack. (See rule [117.3a].)
- State-based actions don’t use the stack. (See rule [405.6f].)
- Exceptions/special cases: the cleanup step normally doesn’t give priority, but if state-based actions would be performed or triggered abilities are waiting (including ones that trigger “at the beginning of the next cleanup step”), those state-based actions are performed and those triggered abilities are put onto the stack, and then the active player gets priority. (See rule [514.3a].) Likewise, when an effect ends the turn or ends the combat phase, the game checks state-based actions but in those specific procedures no player gets priority and no triggered abilities are put onto the stack as part of that ending effect’s resolution. (See rules [724.1c] and [724.2c].)

In short: whenever priority would be given is the normal check point for state-based actions (subject to the ordering around turn-based actions at step/phase starts), plus the stated special-case procedures above.

results.question: when can I concede a game?
results.text:
You may concede a game at any time. Concede is defined as “To quit the game. Conceding a game immediately causes that player to leave that game and lose that game.” [Concede] Conceding is something a player may do at any time (see also rule confirming this applies even outside the stack). [104.3a] [405.6g]

Additional points: a player’s controller can’t make that player concede—conceding is the conceding player’s choice. [723.6] If you concede while playing Two-Headed Giant, your entire team leaves the game immediately and that team loses the game. [810.8b] When a player leaves the game, face-down conspiracy cards controlled by that player are revealed to all players. [702.106e] Also note that a card’s text overrides these rules only where it directly contradicts them, but the exception that a player may concede at any time still applies. [101.1]

Assumption: none needed—the rules explicitly state conceding may happen “at any time.” [104.3a] [Concede]

results.question: how do I know who the active player is?
results.text:
The active player is the player whose turn it is — i.e., the player currently taking their turn. (See rule [102.1].)

Definition and important notes:
- “Active player” = the player whose turn it is. [102.1]
- If the shared team turns option is being used, each team takes turns rather than each player; the team whose turn it is is the active team. [805.4a] The shared team turns option is used in formats such as Two‑Headed Giant. [805.1]
- When multiple players would make choices at the same time, the active player makes any required choices first, then the next player in turn order, etc. (APNAP order). [101.4] [101.4e]
- If an ability refers to “the active player” in a situation with more than one active player, the controller of that ability chooses which active player it refers to when the effect is applied. [805.9]

results.question: when someone other than the active player casts a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text:
The player who cast the spell (even if that player is not the active player) gets priority back first. Priority is the game resource that lets a player cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions [117.1].

Reasoning: a player must have had priority to cast the spell, and rule [117.3c] says that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. That means when a nonactive player casts a spell, that nonactive player (the caster) gets priority before other players. If the spell’s casting process explicitly instructs another player to do something at the same time (for example, choosing modes or targets), follow rule [601.7b] for the order of those choices. After the spell and any responses resolve, the active player receives priority per [117.3b].

results.question: when the active player cast a spell, who gets priority first?
results.text:
Direct answer: Immediately after the active player casts a spell (i.e., takes the casting action while they have priority), that same player — the active player who cast the spell — receives priority first.

Definition of priority: Priority is the game state that allows a player to cast spells, activate abilities, and take special actions (see rule 117.1). Because a player can only cast a spell while they have priority (117.1), rule 117.3c then says that if a player has priority when they cast a spell, that player receives priority afterward. Therefore the active player who cast the spell gets priority first after the casting action completes (117.1, 117.3c).

results.question: can I hold priority to cast more spells after I've cast one or more spells?
results.text: Yes. If you had priority when you began casting a spell, you receive priority again immediately after that spell is cast, so you may cast additional spells (repeat as desired). However, spells you cast because an effect instructs you to cast them during the resolution of another spell or ability do not give you priority afterward. Also note that after a spell or ability resolves, the active player gets priority (so who gets priority after resolution can differ from who had priority while casting).

results.question: when are lore counters put on sagas?
results.text:
Lore counters are put on Saga permanents in two ways: as they enter the battlefield (they enter with lore counter(s) because of an “enters with” replacement effect) and immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins (that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities). When counters are put onto a Saga, its chapter abilities may trigger if their threshold is reached.

Definitions and supporting detail
- Lore counters: Sagas use lore counters to track their progress (they are the counters Sagas use for chapters). [714.3]
- Entering the battlefield: Each Saga without read ahead has the intrinsic replacement ability “This Saga enters with a lore counter on it,” so it enters with one lore counter. [714.3a] Each Saga with read ahead has the intrinsic replacement abilities “As this Saga enters, choose a number between one and this Saga’s final chapter number” and “This Saga enters with the chosen number of lore counters on it.” That choice happens as it enters. [714.3b][702.155b]
- Replacement-effect nature: Abilities that read “[This permanent] enters with . . . ” or “As [this permanent] enters . . . ” are replacement effects. Those replacement effects cause the Saga to enter with the specified number of lore counters. [614.1c]
- Precombat main phase: Immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga enchantment they control that has one or more chapter abilities. This is a turn‑based action that doesn’t use the stack. (See also the related active-player step wording for two‑player turn order.) [714.3c][703.4f][505.4]
- Chapter triggers: A chapter symbol’s triggered ability reads “When one or more lore counters are put onto this Saga, if the number of lore counters on it was less than N and became at least N, [effect],” so chapter abilities can trigger when lore counters are put on the Saga and the chapter’s threshold is reached. [714.2b][107.15a]

Summary timeline (concise):
1) As a Saga enters, replacement effects determine whether it enters with counters (either one for Sagas without read ahead, or the chosen number for Sagas with read ahead). [714.3a][714.3b][702.155b][614.1c]
2) Immediately after a player’s precombat main phase begins, that player puts a lore counter on each Saga they control that has one or more chapter abilities (turn‑based action; no stack). [714.3c][703.4f][505.4]
3) When one or more lore counters are put onto a Saga, chapter abilities whose thresholds are reached may trigger. [714.2b][107.15a]

results.question: what is a delayed triggered ability?
results.text:
A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by some effect that tells the game to do something later (it contains “when,” “whenever,” or “at”) rather than doing it as the creating spell or ability resolves (see rule 603.7). In short: an effect creates the delayed triggered ability during resolution (or as a replacement or via a static ability that allows an action), and that ability waits for its trigger event to occur later. (See rule 603.7a for when they’re created.)

Key points and definitions:
- What it is: A delayed triggered ability is an ability created by another effect that will trigger later and that contains the words “when,” “whenever,” or “at” (rule 603.7 and the heading “Delayed Triggered Ability”).
- When it’s created: Delayed triggered abilities are created during the resolution of spells or abilities, when a replacement effect is applied, or as the result of a static ability that allows an action (rule 603.7a). One-shot effects may create them (rule 610.2).
- Trigger timing and frequency: A delayed triggered ability won’t trigger until it has actually been created, even if its trigger event already happened earlier; it triggers only once (the next time its trigger event happens) unless it has a stated duration such as “this turn” (rule 603.7a and 603.7b). If the trigger event happens more than once simultaneously and there’s no stated duration, the controller of the delayed triggered ability chooses which event causes it to trigger (rule 603.7b).
- Source and controller: If a spell created the delayed triggered ability, the source of that delayed triggered ability is that spell and its controller is the player who controlled that spell as it resolved (rule 603.7d). If an activated or triggered ability created it, its source is the same as that other ability and its controller is the player who controlled that other ability as it resolved (rule 603.7e). If a static ability’s replacement effect created it or a static ability that allowed an action created it, the source is the object with that static ability and its controller is the controller of that object at the time the replacement effect was applied or the action was taken (rules 603.7f and 603.7g). An activated or triggered ability may also create a delayed triggered ability that waits until that ability has resolved a certain number of times in a turn; that delayed triggered ability is created only once during the appropriate resolution (rule 603.7h).
- Interaction with objects and zones: A delayed triggered ability that refers to a particular object still affects that object even if the object’s characteristics change, but if the object is no longer in the expected zone when the delayed triggered ability resolves, the ability won’t affect it (rule 603.7c). Note that objects that change zones become new objects (rule 400.7), which can affect whether the delayed triggered ability can affect them (rule 603.7c).
- X values: If a delayed triggered ability created by a resolving spell or ability refers to X, and X was chosen for that creating spell or ability’s cost, the delayed triggered ability uses the same value of X (rule 107.3n).
- Reflexive cases: Reflexive triggered abilities are a special case of delayed triggered abilities that are created and then checked immediately during the resolution of the creating spell or ability; they follow the delayed triggered ability rules but are checked immediately after creation (rule 603.12).
- When it actually does something: Once a delayed triggered ability has triggered, its controller puts it on the stack the next time a player would receive priority (rule 603.3a). It becomes the topmost object on the stack and functions as a triggered ability normally does (rule 603.3a).

Assumption about multiplayer: The quoted rules do not introduce different handling for multiplayer vs. two-player play for what a delayed triggered ability is; the description above follows the provided rules. If you need how choosing events or controllers works in multiplayer in a specific card context, supply that scenario.

results.question: can non-permanent spells have abilities?
results.text: Yes. Instant and sorcery spells (the non‑permanent spells a player casts that aren’t meant to become permanents) can have abilities: any text on an instant or sorcery card is a spell ability and usually functions while that object is on the stack. Definitions and brief explanation: • “Non‑permanent spell” here means a spell that isn’t a permanent spell (typically an instant or sorcery). • “Spell ability” is an ability followed as an instruction while an instant or sorcery spell is resolving; any text on an instant or sorcery card is a spell ability unless it’s an activated ability, a triggered ability, or a static ability covered by rule 113.6 (see below) [113.3a]. • “Static ability” is an ability that does something continuously rather than being activated or triggered [604.1]. What the rules say and how it works: • Any text on an instant or sorcery card is a spell ability (so instants and sorceries can and do have abilities that function as spell abilities) [113.3a]. • Abilities of an instant or sorcery spell usually function only while that object is on the stack [113.6]. • Some static abilities do apply while a spell is on the stack (for example, those that refer to countering the spell or that modify casting as an additional cost) [604.5]. • Some static abilities apply while a card is in any zone you could cast it from (usually your hand) (for example, “You may cast this card …”) [604.6]. • An object’s ability that restricts or modifies how that particular object can be played or cast functions in any zone from which it could be played or cast and also on the stack; an object’s ability that grants it another ability that restricts or modifies how that particular object can be played or cast functions only on the stack [113.6e]. • A static ability can create a one‑shot effect that causes a spell to gain an ability as you cast it; such gained abilities begin to apply as the spell is put on the stack [610.5, 601.2a]. • When a card is put on the stack as a spell, it has the card’s characteristics (so the spell has the printed text to be a spell ability unless one of the exceptions applies) [601.2a, 405.4]. Contrast with permanent spells: • Abilities printed on non‑instant/sorcery cards (permanent spells) usually function only while that object is on the battlefield rather than while it’s a spell on the stack [113.6]. Summary sentence: instants and sorceries can have and do have abilities (their text is treated as spell abilities that normally function on the stack), while static or other special abilities have limited exceptions enabling them to function on the stack or in other zones in specific cases [113.3a, 113.6, 604.5, 604.6, 113.6e, 610.5, 601.2a, 405.4, 604.1].

results.question: can I use a mana ability when a spell with split-second is on the stack?
results.text: Yes — you may activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack. Split second means “As long as this spell is on the stack, players can’t cast other spells or activate abilities that aren’t mana abilities.” (That’s the definition of split second.) A mana ability is an activated or triggered ability that’s a mana ability; mana abilities follow special rules (they don’t use the stack and are subject to the rules for mana abilities). Because players are explicitly allowed to activate mana abilities while a spell with split second is on the stack, you may do so; non‑mana activated abilities and casting other spells are prohibited while that split second spell is on the stack. Also note that activated mana abilities resolve immediately and don’t use the stack, and you may activate mana abilities whenever you have priority or when a rule or effect asks for a mana payment. Finally, if you had priority before you activated a mana ability, you get priority again after it resolves.

results.question: [Counterspell] is on top of the stack targeting my [Divination]. When everyone passes priority, what resolves first, and does Divination still resolve?
results.text:
Counterspell resolves first; when it resolves it counters Divination, so Divination is put into its owner’s graveyard and does not resolve. 

Why: When all players pass, the object on top of the stack resolves (rule 608.1). The physical card Divination is a spell on the stack (rules 112.1 and 405.1), and Counterspell is the instant on top of the stack (card: Counterspell). As Counterspell resolves, its controller follows its instructions (rule 608.2c); Counterspell’s text is “Counter target spell” (card: Counterspell). To counter a spell means to cancel it so it doesn’t resolve and to put the countered spell into its owner’s graveyard (rule 701.6a). Therefore Divination (card: Divination) is countered when Counterspell resolves and won’t resolve. As the final part of resolving an instant, Counterspell is then put into its owner’s graveyard (rule 608.2n). (Also note the player who cast Divination doesn’t get any refund of costs when Divination is countered — rule 701.6b.)

results.question: My [Charging Rhino] has trample and is blocked by [Vampire Nighthawk], which has deathtouch. How much combat damage do I have to assign to the blocker before I can trample the rest over to the player?
results.text: You must assign at least 3 damage from Charging Rhino to Vampire Nighthawk before you can assign any of Charging Rhino’s remaining damage to the defending player. Explanation: Charging Rhino is a 4/4, so it assigns 4 combat damage equal to its power (see rule 510.1a and card data for Charging Rhino). Trample requires the controller of an attacking creature with trample to assign lethal damage to the creature(s) blocking it before assigning any excess to the player (see rule 702.19b). “Lethal damage” means an amount of damage greater than or equal to a creature’s toughness (see the Lethal Damage definition). Vampire Nighthawk is a 2/3, so lethal damage for Vampire Nighthawk is 3. Vampire Nighthawk’s deathtouch does not reduce the amount Charging Rhino must assign, because the special rule about deathtouch making a small amount count as lethal applies to the source that is dealing damage (see rule 702.2c and 120.4a); Charging Rhino does not have deathtouch (see Charging Rhino card data), so Charging Rhino must assign an amount equal to Vampire Nighthawk’s toughness (3) before any of Charging Rhino’s remaining 1 damage can be assigned to the player.

results.question: I have [Monastery Swiftspear] on the battlefield and I cast [Shardless Agent]. When its cascade ability puts a noncreature spell onto the stack, does Monastery Swiftspear's prowess trigger before or after that cascaded spell resolves?
results.text: Monastery Swiftspear’s prowess will trigger when you cast the spell that you cast via Shardless Agent’s cascade, and the Monastery Swiftspear prowess triggered ability will resolve before that cascaded spell resolves.

results.question: My opponent's [Grizzly Bears] has 2 damage marked on it. Do state-based actions make it die before my [Lightning Bolt] resolves?
results.text:
No — state-based actions don’t automatically destroy Grizzly Bears before Lightning Bolt resolves unless state-based actions have already been checked since the 2 damage was marked. If the 2 damage was already present and state-based actions were checked afterward, Grizzly Bears would already be in its owner’s graveyard and couldn’t be targeted. If the 2 damage was dealt during the resolution of some spell or ability and state-based actions haven’t yet been checked, state-based actions aren’t checked during another spell’s resolution, so Lightning Bolt will resolve while Grizzly Bears is still on the battlefield; Lightning Bolt’s resolution will deal 3 damage to Grizzly Bears, then state-based actions will be checked and Grizzly Bears will be destroyed if it has lethal damage.

Definitions and rules used: A state-based action is a game action that happens automatically whenever certain conditions are met; they don’t use the stack and are performed whenever a player would get priority (state-based actions are defined in rule [704.1] and the checking process is in rule [704.3] and rule [117.5]). “Lethal damage” means damage marked on a creature greater than or equal to its toughness; such a creature is destroyed as a state-based action (see rules [302.7] and [120.6]). State-based actions aren’t checked in the middle of resolving a spell or ability (see rule [704.4]), so a spell currently resolving (Lightning Bolt) will finish resolving before the next state-based-action check. Also, a creature with toughness 0 or less is put into its owner’s graveyard as a state-based action (rule [704.5f]).

Assumption about timing: I assumed you mean “before Lightning Bolt resolves.” If instead you meant “before Lightning Bolt is cast” or “before Lightning Bolt is put on the stack,” the relevant point is that state-based actions are checked whenever a player would get priority, so if state-based actions were checked after the 2 damage was marked, Grizzly Bears would already be dead and Lightning Bolt couldn’t be cast targeting it.

results.question: It's my upkeep. My [Phyrexian Arena]'s beginning-of-upkeep trigger and my opponent's own beginning-of-upkeep trigger both want to go on the stack. Who chooses the order, and when exactly do they trigger?
results.text:
Direct answer: Both triggers (your Phyrexian Arena’s “At the beginning of your upkeep…” triggered ability and your opponent’s beginning-of-upkeep triggered ability) trigger when the upkeep step begins, and they are put onto the stack the next time a player would receive priority (immediately as the upkeep begins). Because multiple triggered abilities that triggered since the last time a player received priority are placed on the stack in APNAP order, you (the active player) put your Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability onto the stack first, then your opponent puts their beginning-of-upkeep triggered ability on the stack on top of it — so your opponent’s ability will resolve before Phyrexian Arena’s.  

Reasoning and key-term definitions (concise):  
- A “triggered ability” is an ability written like “[When/Whenever/At] [trigger condition], [effect]” and it automatically triggers when its trigger event occurs [603.1].  
- Abilities that trigger “at the beginning of” a step (for example, “at the beginning of your upkeep”) trigger when that step begins and they are put on the stack the next time a player would receive priority [500.6].  
- The upkeep step begins and the active player receives priority at that time; any abilities that triggered during the untap step and any abilities that triggered at the beginning of the upkeep are put onto the stack before the active player gets priority [503.1], [117.3a].  
- When multiple triggered abilities have triggered since the last time a player received priority, they are placed on the stack using the process that uses APNAP order: each player, in APNAP order, puts triggered abilities they control that aren’t triggered by other abilities on the stack in any order they choose, then the process continues for remaining triggered abilities [603.3b]. APNAP order means the active player acts first, then the next player in turn order, etc. [101.4].  

Practical outcome for your two triggers:  
- Both triggers occur at the same time (at the beginning of upkeep) [500.6], [603.2b].  
- Because you are the active player, you put Phyrexian Arena’s triggered ability on the stack first; your opponent then puts their beginning-of-upkeep triggered ability on the stack, so your opponent’s ability will be the one to resolve first [603.3b], [101.4].  

If one of the beginning-of-upkeep abilities is optional (contains “may”), it still goes on the stack when it triggers; the choice whether to do the optional effect is made when that ability resolves [603.5].

results.question: I cast a sorcery with buyback and pay its buyback cost, then copy that spell with [Fork]. Once everything resolves, how many copies of the card end up back in my hand?
results.text:
One card — only the original sorcery card returns to your hand; the copy created by Fork doesn’t return a card. Buyback (you paid it when casting the sorcery) causes that spell’s card to be put into its owner’s hand as it resolves instead of into the graveyard, so the physical sorcery card comes back to your hand. Fork puts a copy of that spell onto the stack that isn’t a card (there is no card representing the copy), and a copy that isn’t a card can’t be put into your hand as the spell resolves, so you get nothing from the copy. This is true whether the copy resolves before or after the original spell—the copy isn’t a card and won’t produce a card for your hand, while the original spell’s card does return because you paid buyback.

Definitions
- Buyback: “You may pay an additional [cost] as you cast this spell” and “If the buyback cost was paid, put this spell into its owner’s hand instead of into that player’s graveyard as it resolves.” [702.27a]
- Copy of a spell: A copy of a spell is put onto the stack but isn’t a card; it copies the original spell’s characteristics and decisions, and it isn’t considered to have been cast. [707.10] [707.10b] [707.10d] [Fork ruling #9] [Fork ruling #10]

Short reasoning and timing assumption
- The sorcery card became a spell on the stack when you cast it, and you paid its buyback, so as that spell resolves its card is put into your hand instead of your graveyard. [601.2b] [112.1a] [702.27a]
- When Fork resolves it creates a copy of that spell on the stack that has no physical card associated with it; that copy resolving cannot put a card into your hand. [707.10] [Fork ruling #10] [Fork ruling #8]
- A copy that leaves the stack ceases to exist and does not become a card in any zone. [704.5e]
- I’m assuming the usual stack order (the last thing put on the stack resolves first). The conclusion (one card returns) does not change under the other possible resolution orders because the Fork-created object is never a card. [608.2n]

results.question: I have a face-down manifested card that's really [Lightning Bolt]. It dies and I imprint it on [Mimic Vat]. Later I activate Mimic Vat's copy ability -- do I get a token?
results.text:
No — you won’t get a token. When your face-down manifested card Lightning Bolt died and was exiled by Mimic Vat’s imprint ability, the exiled card is a nonpermanent card (a card not on the battlefield). Rule [110.5d] says cards not on the battlefield are not permanents. Mimic Vat’s ruling [Mimic Vat ruling #0] explicitly covers this situation: if the creature that dies is an instant or sorcery card that was manifested, Mimic Vat may have a nonpermanent card exiled, and you can’t create a token that’s a copy of a nonpermanent card — no token is created. (Mimic Vat’s other ruling [Mimic Vat ruling #4] notes that the token would be a copy of whatever card is exiled when the ability resolves, but that does not allow creating a token from a nonpermanent card in this case.)

Definitions of key terms used above:
- “Nonpermanent card”: a card that is not a permanent — cards not on the battlefield are not permanents ([110.5d]).
- “Manifested” (as used here): a manifested permanent represented by an instant or sorcery card is a face-down object represented by that card; rule [701.40g] describes how such a manifested permanent behaves (for example, it stays face down if it would turn face up).

results.question: My [Fiend Hunter]'s enters-the-battlefield ability is on the stack, about to exile a creature. I copy that ability with [Lithoform Engine] and target a second creature. Both get exiled. When Fiend Hunter later leaves the battlefield, do both come back?
results.text:
Yes — when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield, both creatures exiled by Fiend Hunter’s original enters-the-battlefield ability and the copy of that ability created by Lithoform Engine are returned to the battlefield.

Reasoning: A “linked abilities” pair exists when an object has one ability that exiles one or more cards and another ability that refers to “the exiled card(s)” (see rule 607.1 and rule 607.2a). Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability exiles a creature and Fiend Hunter’s leaves-the-battlefield ability refers to “the exiled card,” so those abilities are linked (607.1; 607.2a). Lithoform Engine’s ruling explicitly states that if Fiend Hunter’s enters-the-battlefield ability is copied, the copy is also linked to Fiend Hunter’s leave-the-battlefield ability and that both exiled creatures return when Fiend Hunter leaves (Lithoform Engine ruling #4). Therefore both creatures come back when Fiend Hunter leaves the battlefield (Fiend Hunter; Lithoform Engine ruling #4; 607.1; 607.2a).

results.question: My own [Banishing Light] has an opponent's creature exiled. On my opponent's turn I cast [Teferi's Protection], phasing out my Banishing Light. Does the exiled creature return to the battlefield?
results.text: The exiled creature stays exiled; it does not return when Banishing Light phases out because phasing isn’t the same as leaving the battlefield. Definition and reasoning: Phasing is a status where a permanent phases out and is treated as though it doesn’t exist while it’s phased out, and when a permanent phases in its status becomes “phased in” again (see rules 702.26d and 702.26c). Phasing doesn’t cause a permanent to change zones or control, and zone-change triggers don’t trigger when a permanent phases in or out (see rule 702.26d). Banishing Light’s ability exiles a target “until this enchantment leaves the battlefield” (Banishing Light). Teferi’s Protection explicitly rules that “Any one-shot effects that are waiting ‘until [this] leaves the battlefield,’ such as that of Banishing Light, won’t happen when a permanent phases out” (Teferi’s Protection ruling #21). Therefore, when Teferi’s Protection causes Banishing Light to phase out, that doesn’t count as Banishing Light leaving the battlefield and the “until Banishing Light leaves the battlefield” condition does not occur; the exiled creature remains exiled. The creature will remain exiled unless and until Banishing Light actually leaves the battlefield (not merely phases out).

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. In response to its cast trigger, my opponent tries to [Counterspell] it. Can they even target it given protection from instants, and if it's countered, do I still control their next turn?
results.text:
Yes. Your opponent can cast Counterspell targeting Emrakul, the Promised End while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack, and if Counterspell successfully counters Emrakul, the Promised End the triggered “When you cast this spell” ability still exists and will resolve (so you will gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn and then that player will take an extra turn) unless that triggered ability is itself countered or otherwise prevented.

Reasoning and definitions (short):
- “Protection from instants” in this situation: Emrakul, the Promised End’s protection from instants means Emrakul, the Promised End can’t be the target of instant spells while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield, but that protection applies only while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the battlefield ([Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #1]; [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]). Emrakul, the Promised End as a spell on the stack is not on the battlefield, so that protection does not stop an instant from targeting the spell on the stack. (The physical card Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack when you cast it [405.1], and a spell described as a “spell” refers to a spell on the stack [109.2b].)
- “Target”: targets for spells and abilities are chosen as part of putting that spell or ability on the stack ([115.1a]; see the casting steps in 601.2a and 601.2c).
- Triggered ability timing: Emrakul, the Promised End’s triggered ability (“When you cast this spell...”) is created when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End and triggers at that time; it is a separate triggered ability that will be put on the stack and resolve independently of whether Emrakul, the Promised End later resolves or is countered ([601.2i]; [603.1a]).

How the sequence you described works given those points:
- You cast Emrakul, the Promised End; the card becomes a spell on the stack ([601.2a]; [405.1]). The “When you cast this spell” ability triggers at that time ([601.2i]; [603.1a]).
- Your opponent may cast Counterspell (an instant) in response to the triggered ability (or in response to the spell) and may target the Emrakul, the Promised End spell on the stack because Emrakul, the Promised End’s protection from instants does not apply while Emrakul, the Promised End is on the stack ([Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #2]; [109.2b]; [115.1a]).
- If Counterspell resolves and successfully counters the Emrakul, the Promised End spell, that removes the Emrakul, the Promised End spell from the stack; that does not undo the triggered ability that was created when you cast Emrakul, the Promised End. The triggered ability will still be on the stack (or be put on the stack) and will resolve unless something else counters or prevents that ability ([601.2i]; [603.1a]). When that triggered ability resolves it will perform its controller-changing and extra-turn effects as written on Emrakul, the Promised End’s card text (Emrakul, the Promised End). (If another effect later replaces or overwrites the player-controlling effect, the last-created such effect is the one that applies [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14].)

A couple brief clarifications:
- If your opponent tried to target the triggered ability itself with Counterspell, that wouldn’t work because Counterspell targets a spell and activated/triggered abilities on the stack aren’t spells and can’t be targeted by something that only targets spells ([113.9]).
- This answer assumes the opponent cast Counterspell targeting the Emrakul, the Promised End spell while Emrakul, the Promised End’s triggered ability had already been created by the cast; if the timing were different (for example, if you somehow didn’t create the triggered ability), the result could differ.

results.question: My cascade spell exiles cards until it hits [Valki, God of Lies], whose back face is the seven-mana planeswalker Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor. Is that a legal cascade hit, and can I cast the Tibalt side for free?
results.text:
Yes. Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor can be the card that stops the cascade (it’s a legal cascade hit), but you may not cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free unless that face’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value. You may cast Valki, God of Lies (the front face) for free if Valki, God of Lies’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value.

Reasoning and definitions (short):
- Cascade: When you cast a spell with cascade, you exile cards from the top of your library until you exile a nonland card whose mana value is less than that cascade spell’s mana value; you then may cast that card without paying its mana cost if the resulting spell’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value. [702.85a]
- A double-faced card: it’s a card with two faces. Modal double-faced cards (such as Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor) have two faces you can choose between when an effect lets you play or cast the card from a group of cards. [712.1] [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16]
- Exiled cards are face up by default, so you can see that the exiled card is Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor and choose a face that fits the effect. [406.3b]

How the rules apply here:
- The cascade exile step looks at the exiled card’s mana value to decide when to stop; Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a legal card to stop on if that card’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value. [702.85a]
- After exile, cascade lets you cast that card without paying its mana cost only if the resulting spell’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value. If you choose to cast the back face Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor, that resulting spell’s mana value is the mana value of Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (7), and that must be less than the cascade spell’s mana value to be legal. [702.85a] [712.11c]
- Because Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor is a modal double-faced card and an effect that lets you cast a card from among exiled cards lets you choose a face, you may attempt to cast either face—but the chosen face is evaluated for legality (including its mana value) when determining whether you may cast it for free. [Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16] [712.11c] [601.3e]

Therefore: the card is a valid cascade hit, but you cannot cast the Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor face for free unless Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value; you can cast Valki, God of Lies (the front face) for free if Valki, God of Lies’s mana value is less than the cascade spell’s mana value.

If you want a concrete example, say your cascade spell’s mana value is 5: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (card MV 2) will stop the cascade, you may cast Valki, God of Lies (MV 2) for free, but you may not cast Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor (MV 7) for free because 7 is not less than 5.
citations: Valki, God of Lies // Tibalt, Cosmic Impostor ruling #16

results.question: I cast [Emrakul, the Promised End]. With its cast trigger on the stack, I copy that trigger with [Lithoform Engine]. Then I untap Lithoform Engine with [Voltaic Key] and use it again to copy [Emrakul, the Promised End] itself as a permanent spell. How many of my opponent's turns do I control, do I get a second Emrakul, and does copying the Emrakul spell give me another control-a-turn trigger?
results.text:
Direct answer: You will control your opponent for only one of that player’s turns (their “next turn”), you will get a second Emrakul, the Promised End as a token when the copied permanent spell resolves, and copying the Emrakul, the Promised End spell with Lithoform Engine does NOT create an additional “When you cast this spell” trigger (but your earlier copy of the cast trigger does give you a second trigger). 

Why: • When you cast Emrakul, the Promised End, its “When you cast this spell …” triggered ability is created and put on the stack (casting the card creates that triggered ability) [601.2i]. • You used Lithoform Engine’s first ability to copy that triggered ability on the stack; a copy of a triggered ability is itself an ability on the stack and will resolve like the original copy did (so you now have two instances of the Emrakul, the Promised End triggered ability on the stack) [707.10; Lithoform Engine ruling #3]. • Each resolved instance of Emrakul, the Promised End’s triggered ability will create the same pair of effects (you gain control of the targeted opponent during that player’s next turn, and after that turn that player takes an extra turn). Multiple such abilities will each create the extra turn(s) [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. • However, multiple player-controlling effects that affect the same player overwrite one another; the last such effect to be created is the one that actually grants control for that turn. So although you will have two triggered abilities that each produce an extra turn, only the last-created player-control effect determines which one of those (the single) next turns you actually control [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14]. Which trigger’s control effect “wins” depends on which triggered ability is created last (that corresponds to the order the triggers resolve). 

• Separately, when you untapped Lithoform Engine with Voltaic Key and used Lithoform Engine’s {4},{T} ability to copy the Emrakul, the Promised End permanent spell, that ability puts a copy of the permanent spell onto the stack rather than causing you to cast it; a copy of a spell isn’t cast (Lithoform Engine’s copy is created on the stack) [707.10; Lithoform Engine ruling #6]. Because it isn’t cast, that copy does not cause Emrakul, the Promised End’s “When you cast this spell …” triggered ability to be created. 

• When the copied permanent spell resolves it becomes a token permanent that has the characteristics of Emrakul, the Promised End (you therefore get a second Emrakul, the Promised End token) [Lithoform Engine card text and ruling #6; 111.13]. 

Timing note/assumption: I assumed the scenario you described (you copied the cast trigger first, then later copied the Emrakul, the Promised End spell). Which of the two triggered abilities’ control effects ultimately applies is determined by which of those triggered abilities is created last (i.e., which resolves later); the ruling above (only one control effect applies) still holds either way [Emrakul, the Promised End ruling #14].

results.question: I've imprinted a creature on [Mimic Vat] and activate its ability to make a token copy. While that ability is on the stack, I copy it with [Lithoform Engine]. Do I get two tokens?
results.text:
Yes — you get two tokens. Copying Mimic Vat’s activated ability with Lithoform Engine puts a second instance of that ability onto the stack, and each instance can create a token when it resolves.

Reasoning and definition of key term:
- “To copy ... an activated ability” means to put a copy of that ability onto the stack; a copy of an activated ability isn’t activated and is itself an ability (see [707.10] and [707.10b]).
- Lithoform Engine’s first ability, when it targets an activated ability on the stack, creates another instance of that ability on the stack (see [Lithoform Engine ruling #3]).
- Mimic Vat’s activated ability reads “{3}, {T}: Create a token that's a copy of a card exiled with this artifact. It gains haste. Exile it at the beginning of the next end step.” The token created by that ability will be a copy of whatever card is exiled with Mimic Vat at the time the ability resolves (see [Mimic Vat ruling #4]).

Put together: you activated Mimic Vat’s ability (one instance on the stack) and then used Lithoform Engine to copy that ability, which placed a second instance of the same ability on the stack. When each instance resolves, it attempts to create a token that’s a copy of the card currently exiled with Mimic Vat, so you can get two tokens (one from each resolving instance). If no card is exiled with Mimic Vat when a particular instance resolves, that instance creates no token (see [Mimic Vat ruling #6]).

Timing note: this assumes both instances resolve (order depends on how they were put on the stack). If the card exiled with Mimic Vat changes between the two resolutions, each resolving instance will create a token copy of whatever is exiled at its own resolution (see [Mimic Vat ruling #4]).

results.question: An opponent controls an untapped [Trinisphere], and I have a permanent that makes my green spells cost {1} less. I want to cast [Awaken the Woods] for value. If I cast it with X=0, what does it cost and what do I get, and what X should I actually choose?
results.text:
If you cast Awaken the Woods with X=0 while an opponent controls an untapped Trinisphere and you have a permanent that makes your green spells cost {1} less, the spell’s locked-in total cost will be {1}{G}{G} and you will create 0 tokens. You should choose X=2 (not X=0); choosing X=2 will also lock in a total cost of {1}{G}{G} but will create two 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens, so X=2 is strictly better value than X=0 (and better than X=1) for the same total cost.

Reasoning and assumptions
- X is the variable in Awaken the Woods’ mana cost; a player announces the value of X as part of casting the spell (you choose X when you cast Awaken the Woods) [601.2b]. Awaken the Woods’s effect creates X 1/1 green Forest Dryad land creature tokens, so X=0 produces zero tokens (Awaken the Woods card text).
- To determine the total cost you will pay, start with the mana cost you are paying (including the chosen X), add any cost increases, then apply cost reductions, and finally apply Trinisphere’s effect if the mana component is less than three mana (Trinisphere ruling #0; the casting/total-cost procedure in 601.2f).
- The permanent that “makes my green spells cost {1} less” is a cost-reduction effect that affects only the spell’s generic-mana component (effects that reduce generic mana affect only the generic component) [118.7a]. That means such a reduction can only reduce the numeric generic portion of the cost; it cannot reduce green ({G}) symbols.
- Case X=0: the mana cost you start with is {G}{G}. The {1} green-spell cost reduction can’t reduce any generic because there is no generic portion when X=0, so after reductions the cost is still {G}{G}. Trinisphere then applies because the mana component is 2, which is less than three, and raises the spell’s mana component to a total of three mana by adding generic mana as needed. The resulting locked-in total cost is {1}{G}{G}. Paying that cost creates 0 tokens because X was announced as 0 [601.2b; Trinisphere ruling #0; Awaken the Woods].
- Case X=1: start with {1}{G}{G}; the {1} generic reduction reduces the generic {1} to {0}, leaving {G}{G}; Trinisphere then raises the mana component to three, producing a locked-in cost of {1}{G}{G} — for one token. (Same total cost as X=0 but produces one token.)
- Case X=2: start with {2}{G}{G}; the {1} generic reduction reduces the generic {2} to {1}, leaving {1}{G}{G}. Because that mana component totals three, Trinisphere does not change it. The locked-in total cost is {1}{G}{G}, and you get two tokens. That is strictly better (more tokens for the same cost) than X=0 or X=1.
- Case X≥3: start with {X}{G}{G}; after the {1} generic reduction the generic portion is X−1. For X≥3 that leaves at least {2} generic (for X=3 it leaves {2}{G}{G}), so the total cost after reductions is greater than three and Trinisphere doesn’t apply; those choices cost more mana than the X=2 case.

Therefore, do not pick X=0. If your goal is to maximize tokens per mana under these effects, choose X=2 (if you can pay the resulting cost) because it gives two tokens for the same locked-in total cost {1}{G}{G} that X=0 would cost while X=0 yields zero tokens.

If you want a different tradeoff (fewer tokens for less outlay of actual available mana), pick whatever X you can actually pay; the text above assumes you can pay the locked-in totals shown. If you can’t actually pay {1}{G}{G}, adjust accordingly.

Assumptions about ambiguous wording
- I treated “makes my green spells cost {1} less” as a generic-mana reduction that can only reduce the generic portion of the cost (per 118.7a). If that cost-reduction instead specifically said “green mana” and reduced green mana symbols, the interaction with Trinisphere could differ; the provided rules don’t include a different cost-reduction effect, so the generic interpretation above is used.

results.question: [Grist, the Hunger Tide] is in my graveyard. Can I return it with [Animate Dead], and what happens?
results.text:
Yes. You can target and return Grist, the Hunger Tide from your graveyard with Animate Dead, but Grist, the Hunger Tide will enter the battlefield as a planeswalker (not a creature), Animate Dead won’t be able to remain attached and will be put into your graveyard; Animate Dead’s delayed triggered ability will trigger but won’t cause Grist, the Hunger Tide to be sacrificed because Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature on the battlefield.

Reasoning and key definitions:
- “Creature card in a graveyard”: Grist, the Hunger Tide is a creature card while it’s not on the battlefield, so it is a legal target for Animate Dead (see Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1 and Animate Dead ruling #1). [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1] [Animate Dead ruling #1]
- Animate Dead’s entered-the-battlefield sequence: When Animate Dead enters the battlefield attached to that creature card, its triggered instruction returns the enchanted creature card to the battlefield and attempts to attach Animate Dead to it (Animate Dead ruling #1). [Animate Dead ruling #1]
- New object / creature status on entering: When Grist, the Hunger Tide is returned to the battlefield it becomes a new object and, per Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1, it is no longer a creature on the battlefield and is just a planeswalker. [400.7] [Grist, the Hunger Tide ruling #1]
- Failure to be a legal Aura attachment: Because Animate Dead’s replacement makes it “enchant [a] creature put onto the battlefield with this Aura,” Animate Dead cannot legally attach to Grist, the Hunger Tide once Grist, the Hunger Tide is on the battlefield as a noncreature planeswalker. When an Aura can’t legally attach in that situation, Animate Dead is put into the graveyard as a state-based action and its delayed triggered ability triggers; when that delayed trigger resolves, “if the creature’s still on the battlefield, its controller sacrifices it” (Animate Dead ruling #4). In this case Grist, the Hunger Tide is not a creature on the battlefield, so that “if the creature’s still on the battlefield” condition is not true and no sacrifice occurs. [Animate Dead ruling #4]

Assumption about timing: This answer assumes the normal resolution of Animate Dead’s entered-the-battlefield effect (Animate Dead is on the battlefield as its triggered ability resolves). If Animate Dead were somehow not on the battlefield when its triggered ability resolved, Animate Dead ruling #0 says none of the return/attach effects would happen. [Animate Dead ruling #0]

TLDR: Yes — Animate Dead can return Grist, the Hunger Tide, but Grist, the Hunger Tide will be a planeswalker on the battlefield, Animate Dead can’t stay attached and goes to your graveyard, and the subsequent delayed trigger won’t make you sacrifice Grist, the Hunger Tide.

results.question: My commander [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] has four +1/+1 counters on it. It dies, I move it to the command zone, then recast it. Does it keep the counters, and does [Doubling Season] double them as it re-enters?
results.text:
Yes. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave keeps its four +1/+1 counters when you move it to the command zone and when you recast it, and Doubling Season does not double those retained counters as it re-enters.

Reasoning and rules applied:
- Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s printed ability and rulings say that counters remain on Skullbriar as it moves to any zone other than a player’s hand or library and that counters that remain aren’t “placed” on Skullbriar (so they persist across zones and are not considered put onto it). See Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #1, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #3, and Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2.
- In a Commander game you may replace an event that would put Skullbriar, the Walking Grave into a hand or library by putting it into the command zone instead; that is allowed by rule 903.9b. When you do so, Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s counters remain on it per its own text and rulings (so the card in the command zone will still have the four +1/+1 counters).
- Doubling Season’s text and rulings apply when an effect “would put one or more counters on a permanent” or when a permanent “enters with counters” (Doubling Season ruling #2). However, because Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s counters weren’t “put” on it as it entered (they “remained” on it), the retained counters aren’t affected by Doubling Season (Skullbriar, the Walking Grave ruling #2). 
- (Background: the general rule is that objects become new objects when they change zones, so counters normally wouldn’t persist; see rule 400.7 and rule 122.2. Skullbriar, the Walking Grave’s card text and rulings create the exception that causes its counters to remain and clarifies how those retained counters interact with effects like Doubling Season.)

results.question: I cast [Final Fortune] to take an extra turn. During that extra turn I use [Sundial of the Infinite] to end the turn before the end step. Do I still lose the game?
results.text: No — you do not lose the game. Because you activated Sundial of the Infinite during the extra turn created by Final Fortune and ended that turn before its end step, the “At the beginning of that turn’s end step, you lose the game.” triggered ability from Final Fortune won’t get a chance to trigger that turn; ending the turn this way skips the end step and prevents “at the beginning of the end step” triggers from triggering, so the lose-the-game trigger will wait until the next time an end step begins. See reasoning and citations below.

results.question: I cast [Clone]. When and how do I choose what it copies, and can my opponent respond to that choice?
results.text:
You choose what Clone copies as Clone is entering the battlefield — the controller of Clone makes the “as this enters the battlefield” choice while applying Clone’s replacement effect, and that choice is not made on the stack so opponents don’t get to respond to the choice itself. Opponents can, however, respond to the Clone spell while it’s still a spell on the stack before it resolves (they can’t respond to the post-resolution “as enters” choice). You may only choose a creature that is already on the battlefield when Clone is entering; you may also choose not to copy anything. (Clone’s copy choice does not target.)

Reasoning and definitions
- “As this enters the battlefield” choice: this is a choice made while applying a replacement effect that modifies how the object enters the battlefield; the controller of the entering object makes that choice (see 707.6). 707.6 shows that when an object enters as a copy of another permanent, the entering object’s controller gets to make any “as . . . enters” choices for it. 
- The choice is made as Clone enters the battlefield (not while casting the Clone spell), because it’s an “as this enters” replacement effect that determines Clone’s copiable values as it enters (see 707.2 and 707.6). 616.1c shows that if replacement effects that would cause an object to become a copy as it enters are relevant, one such replacement effect must be chosen when applying those effects. 
- Practical constraints from Clone’s rulings: you can choose only a creature that’s already on the battlefield (Clone ruling #2); you may choose not to copy anything (Clone ruling #5); and Clone’s ability does not target the chosen creature (Clone ruling #0), so protective or targeting responses directed at a “target” of Clone’s choice are not applicable.

Timing assumption note: I’m assuming the normal case where Clone resolves and then enters the battlefield. If Clone were prevented from entering the battlefield (for example, an effect replaced or prevented that event), the choice would be irrelevant because Clone wouldn’t enter to have that choice applied.

results.question: I activate my [Flooded Strand]'s ability, then activate [Gogo, Master of Mimicry] with X=2 to copy it twice. How many lands do I get from that one Flooded Strand?
results.text:
You get up to three lands. Gogo, Master of Mimicry (with X=2) creates two additional instances of the Flooded Strand activated ability on the stack, so the two copies plus the original ability will each resolve separately; each resolution lets you search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle (subject to how many eligible cards remain). 

Reasoning and definitions (rules used):
- “To copy … an activated ability” means putting a copy of that ability onto the stack; the copy is itself an ability and it copies the characteristics and decisions of the original ability ([707.10]).
- Gogo, Master of Mimicry’s ability targets an activated ability on the stack and creates one or more additional instances of that ability on the stack ([Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #6]); the copies’ source is the same as the original ability’s source ([Gogo, Master of Mimicry ruling #9]).
- When copies are created, they are put onto the stack (the controller chooses the order for the copies) and so those copies will resolve as separate abilities on the stack ([707.10d]).
- Flooded Strand’s activated ability reads “{T}, Pay 1 life, Sacrifice this land: Search your library for a Plains or Island card, put it onto the battlefield, then shuffle.” Because each resolving instance of that ability includes its own “then shuffle,” you will perform a full search-and-shuffle for each resolution; the special case that combines multiple searches into a single search applies only when an effect instructs a player to search the library multiple times before instructing that player to shuffle ([701.23h]).

Timing assumption and alternative: I’m assuming you activated Flooded Strand’s ability and then Gogo, Master of Mimicry resolved, creating two copies that were placed on the stack above the original ability (so the two copies resolve first, then the original). If, hypothetically, multiple search instructions were somehow to occur without any intervening shuffle, rule [701.23h] would treat those multiple instructions as a single search; that does not occur in the normal sequence described above.

Cards referenced: Flooded Strand; Gogo, Master of Mimicry.
